question: What is a 'covenant' (berith) in Old Testament theology?

choices.A: A solemn, binding agreement between God and his people involving mutual obligations, promises, and often a ratification ceremony
choices.B: A simple oral contract between two human parties with no religious significance
choices.C: A land grant issued by a king with no obligations attached to it
choices.D: A legal document that was regularly renegotiated every seven years

teaching.title: Covenant (Berith) in the OT
teaching.body: The covenant (Hebrew: berith) is the central organizing concept of the OT. It is a solemn bond creating a family-like relationship between parties with stipulations and promises backed by oath. OT covenants typically involve: a preamble identifying the parties, historical prologue, stipulations, blessings and curses, and a ratification ceremony (often involving divided animals — hence 'cutting' a covenant, karath berith, e.g., Gen 15). The progressive covenant sequence — Noahic, Abrahamic, Mosaic, Davidic, New — structures salvation history and reaches its fulfillment in Christ (the mediator of a New Covenant, Heb 9:15).
refs: Scott Hahn, A Father Who Keeps His Promises
